Full-thickness burns: 1

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A thermal injury leaves dry leathery skin with a pale or charred center and little central sensation. Which burn-depth category best explains destruction of the entire dermis rather than a painful superficial blister alone?

  1. Superficial epidermal burn
  2. Superficial partial-thickness burn
  3. Deep partial-thickness burn
  4. Burn extending into deeper structures
  5. Full-thickness burn
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Full-thickness burn

Destruction of the full dermis produces a dry leathery wound that may be insensate centrally.

Understanding the options

Full-thickness burn
Destruction of the full dermis produces a dry leathery wound that may be insensate centrally.
Superficial epidermal burn
A superficial burn affects epidermis, is often red and painful, and does not form the typical dermal blister pattern. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Superficial partial-thickness burn
A moist, pink, blistered and very painful wound with preserved blanching suggests superficial dermal involvement. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Deep partial-thickness burn
Deeper dermal injury may appear pale or mottled with reduced blanching and sensation and can require surgery. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Burn extending into deeper structures
Fourth-degree terminology describes extension beyond skin into tissue such as muscle, tendon or bone. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
